title: Regulatory Reporting and Data Collection
summary: How authorities design what data they collect, in what form and how often, and the shift from template returns towards granular, standardised and machine-readable reporting.
contentGaps: Written as part of a programme: Aim and Purpose is the module's one-line description; audience, prior knowledge and core reading come from the programme

sections.Aim and Purpose: How authorities design what data they collect, in what form and how often, and the shift from template returns towards granular, standardised and machine-readable reporting.
Learning Objectives: Explain the design choices in regulatory reporting frameworks
Assess the costs and benefits of granular and machine-readable reporting
Evaluate validation, quality checks and feedback loops with reporting firms
Syllabus: Template returns, granular data and data-pull models
Data standards and identifiers: taxonomies, LEI and common data dictionaries
Validation rules, resubmissions and data quality feedback to firms
Reducing reporting burden while improving supervisory value
Intended Audience: Supervisors and analysts who use regulatory returns, risk scores and dashboards in their day-to-day work
Data, statistics, IT and SupTech teams building the authority's data and analytics capability
Heads of department and senior managers responsible for supervisory strategy, resourcing and technology investment
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Some experience of financial supervision or working with regulatory data is helpful. No programming or data science background is required.
Core Reading: BIS Financial Stability Institute, Innovative Technology in Financial Supervision (Suptech): The Experience of Early Users (FSI Insights No 9, 2018)
FSB, The Use of Supervisory and Regulatory Technology by Authorities and Regulated Institutions (2020)
Basel Committee, Principles for Effective Risk Data Aggregation and Risk Reporting (BCBS 239) (2013)
